nameStory: Gattinger's panic grass honors Augustin Gattinger, a 19th-century German-American botanist who spent decades documenting Tennessee's flora. The word 'panic' comes from the Latin 'panicum,' an ancient name for millet, though it has nothing to do with anxiety! Like many plants named after botanists, this grass carries forward the legacy of someone who devoted their life to understanding the natural world.
description: Gattinger's panic grass is a small, delicate annual grass that rarely grows taller than your knee. This wispy member of the grass family forms loose, spreading clumps with slender stems and narrow leaves that sway gently in the breeze. Its tiny flowers are arranged in open, branching clusters that look almost cloud-like when backlit by sunlight. As an annual, it completes its entire life cycle in one growing season, making it somewhat ephemeral in the landscape.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers arranged in loose, open clusters (panicles) that feel delicate and airy to the touch, with small spikelets that turn purplish-bronze as they mature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, soft leaves about pencil-width or thinner, with a smooth texture that feels like silk when you run your fingers along the blade

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that forms small tufts or patches, typically staying under 2 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, smooth stems that bend easily without breaking and often have a slightly flattened feel when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, oval seeds that fall easily from the plant when mature, creating a subtle rustling sound when the grass is disturbed

habitat: **Note: Information about habitat is uncertain due to extremely limited observations in New England.** Based on its known preferences elsewhere, Gattinger's panic grass likely grows in disturbed soils, open areas, and edges of fields or roadsides. It may prefer sandy or well-drained soils and areas with some disturbance that reduces competition from larger plants.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as the soil warms, appearing as small tufts of narrow, bright green leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: The grass reaches its full height and produces its characteristic airy flower clusters, which are most visible from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and begin to drop, while the entire plant starts to turn golden-brown and becomes more brittle to the touch.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following year.

funFact: **Uncertain claim:** Gattinger's panic grass may be one of the rarest grasses in New England, with potentially only a single documented location, making any sighting a genuinely special botanical discovery that could contribute valuable information to our understanding of the region's flora.
confusionNotes: **Uncertain information:** Gattinger's panic grass can be easily confused with other small panic grasses like Philadelphia panic grass, which tends to be more upright, or witch grass, which typically grows much larger. The key is looking for its particularly delicate, open flower clusters and low, spreading growth habit.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, finding Gattinger's panic grass would be like discovering botanical treasure. Many panic grasses look quite similar, and proper identification often requires close examination of tiny flower parts, so any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists or naturalist groups.
compareHints: **Uncertain comparisons:** Compared to its relatives, Gattinger's panic grass is typically smaller and more delicate than switchgrass, less weedy-looking than witch grass, and has more open, airy flower clusters than the denser-flowered smooth witchgrass. Its low, spreading growth habit also sets it apart from the more upright Philadelphia panic grass.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Switchgrass stands out from its panic grass relatives by its impressive size and clumping growth habit - most other Panicum species in New England are much smaller annual weeds.
Witch grass stands out from its Panicum relatives by its distinctive tumbleweed habit and proportionally enormous seed head.
Among the panicgrasses in New England, smooth witchgrass is the most sprawling and has the most open, airy seed head.
Among its panicgrass relatives in New England, bitter panicgrass stands out as the giant of the family and the only one adapted to coastal life.
Unlike its wild native relatives like switchgrass and witch grass, proso millet has much larger, rounder seeds and broader leaves.
Among the panicgrasses, Philadelphia panic grass is the most delicate and smallest.
